explanations.answer: Strike them so the thresholds shake
explanations.explanation: That's the order, friend. The Lord says, "Strike the tops of the pillars so that the thresholds shake." (Amos 9:1) Then the pillars come down on the heads of all the people. I think this is one of those moments where you just hold your breath and keep reading.

explanations.answer: Wash them so the altar stays clean
explanations.explanation: I get it, I like a clean counter too. But nobody is scrubbing anything here. The Lord says, "Strike the tops of the pillars so that the thresholds shake." (Amos 9:1) This is no cleaning job, and the thresholds are about to feel it.

explanations.answer: Coat them so the gold shines bright
explanations.explanation: Ha! If only it were a polish job. I'd bring my own rag. But the Lord says, "Strike the tops of the pillars so that the thresholds shake." (Amos 9:1) Nothing gets shined here. The pillars get struck, and the whole place shakes.

I see why you'd hope so, friend. But the Lord says the opposite: "None of those who flee will get away; none of the fugitives will escape." (Amos 9:1) Not a few, none. Running doesn't open a back door in this verse.

Right, and it's a heavy line. The Lord says, "None of those who flee will get away; none of the fugitives will escape." (Amos 9:1) Nobody slips out, not even one. I think that's the whole point of this stretch: there is no running from Him.

That's it. The Lord says, "though they climb up to heaven, from there I will pull them down." (Amos 9:2) Down in Sheol, up in heaven, same result. Both directions are covered, and nobody gets a free pass for going the extra mile.

explanations.answer: Leave them up there for good
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but nobody gets to park up there. The Lord says, "though they climb up to heaven, from there I will pull them down." (Amos 9:2) Climbing up is no safer than digging down. Either way, His hand finds them.

No gates in this verse, friend. The Lord says, "though they climb up to heaven, from there I will pull them down." (Amos 9:2) He doesn't lock anyone in. He pulls them down, and that's the end of that hiding spot.

Yep, the serpent. The Lord says, "there I will command the serpent to bite them." (Amos 9:3) Notice He's at the bottom of the sea and still has a serpent ready to take orders. Even down there, nobody's hiding.

A lion is a good guess, because it's a scary pick. But the Lord says, "there I will command the serpent to bite them." (Amos 9:3) Besides, we're at the bottom of the sea. A lion down there would need a snorkel.

I can see a bear showing up in a scary verse. But the Lord says, "there I will command the serpent to bite them." (Amos 9:3) It's the bottom of the sea, friend, and bears don't do deep water. It's a serpent, and the Lord is the one who commands it.
That's right. The Lord says, "I will fix My eyes upon them for harm and not for good." (Amos 9:4) It's a hard line to read. I think it fits everything before it, because there's no hiding spot left.

Careful here, friend. It's the other way around. The Lord says, "I will fix My eyes upon them for harm and not for good." (Amos 9:4) This isn't a kind look in this verse. It's the opposite, and it's a sobering one.

Melts, yes. The text says the Lord GOD of Hosts is the One "who touches the earth and it melts." (Amos 9:5) One touch. I can't even touch a hot cookie sheet without a fuss, and He touches the whole earth.

Burning is a fair guess, since I've burned plenty of batches myself. But the text says the Lord GOD of Hosts is the One "who touches the earth and it melts." (Amos 9:5) It melts, and all its dwellers mourn.

I love the cheerful guess, friend, but that's not how this verse goes. The text says the Lord GOD of Hosts is the One "who touches the earth and it melts." (Amos 9:5) It melts, and all its dwellers mourn. Nobody's handing out flowers here.
True. The text says, "He summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth." (Amos 9:6) The sea answers when He calls. And then comes the line, "The LORD is His name."

This one is true, friend. The text says, "He summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth." (Amos 9:6) The sea comes when He calls. I can't even get my timer to listen to me.

The Philistines, yes. The LORD says, "Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir?" (Amos 9:7) Israel isn't the only people He has brought up from somewhere. I think that's worth sitting with for a minute.

The Moabites are a good guess, since they're in the Bible. But they aren't named here. The LORD says, "Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir?" (Amos 9:7) It's the Philistines who come up from Caphtor.

The Edomites do show up in the Bible, but not in this verse. The LORD says, "Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir?" (Amos 9:7) Caphtor goes with the Philistines.

I see why you'd say that, after all those hard lines. But the LORD says, "Yet I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob." (Amos 9:8) The sinful kingdom gets destroyed, and Jacob's house is not utterly destroyed. Pay attention to that word "not."

False, and it's a big turn. The LORD says, "Yet I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob." (Amos 9:8) The sinful kingdom meets its end, but Jacob's house is not utterly destroyed. I think that "Yet" is where you can finally breathe a little.

explanations.answer: Not one will reach the ground
explanations.explanation: Yes, not even a pebble. The LORD says He will shake Israel like grain in a sieve, "but not a pebble will reach the ground." (Amos 9:9) Nothing slips through. I once lost a whole sprinkle jar down a drain and I'm still not over it.

Crushing sounds like it fits the mood. But it isn't what the verse says. The LORD says He will shake Israel like grain in a sieve, "but not a pebble will reach the ground." (Amos 9:9) Not one hits the ground.

explanations.answer: All will fall to the ground
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what you'd expect from a sieve, and the verse flips it too. The LORD says He will shake Israel like grain in a sieve, "but not a pebble will reach the ground." (Amos 9:9) None hit the ground, friend, not even one.

explanations.answer: Those who say disaster will never reach them
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD says, "All the sinners among My people will die by the sword—all those who say, ‘Disaster will never draw near or confront us.’" (Amos 9:10) Those words are the ones He points to. I think it's a good reminder to be careful of saying "it won't happen to me."

explanations.answer: Those who say the LORD has gone silent
explanations.explanation: That sounds like something people might say, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, "All the sinners among My people will die by the sword—all those who say, ‘Disaster will never draw near or confront us.’" (Amos 9:10) The line He points to is about disaster never coming near.

explanations.answer: Those who say the prophets are lying
explanations.explanation: It's a fair guess, because Amos was telling people hard things. But the verse doesn't say that. The LORD says, "All the sinners among My people will die by the sword—all those who say, ‘Disaster will never draw near or confront us.’" (Amos 9:10) The quote is about disaster never drawing near.
